scenario: AITA for telling an intern to throw her banana peel in the trash? | A few details to set the stage: To get into my place of work, one needs to walk from the parking lot down a sidewalk that is along the side of the building. The other side of the sidewalk is semi-wooded with low growing evergreen shrubs. This sidewalk is about 100ft long, and has a trash can at either end. Also, in the last month, there have been a ton of flies buzzing around this area, so much so that the building manager called an exterminator. This morning, I (\~30s F) witnessed an intern (20s F) for one of the companies in our building walking into work eating a banana. About 3/4 of the way down the sidewalk, with a trashcan not even 25 feet away, she tossed the banana peel into the bushes. It landed on top of the bush and she just kept walking. I wasn't sufficiently caffeinated to be polite, so I blurted out "What the hell? There's a trash can right in front of you!" complete with the WTF hand gesture; pointing to the trash can. She ripped into me, claiming it's organic and feeds the animals. She was half yelling / half crying. I pointed at the peel sitting on top of the bush and told her to "pick up your (her) damn banana peel." Instead she cried loudly saying something unintelligible, got her peel, and put it in the trash. I'm thinking, great, this is over. Maybe she won't toss her banana debris into the bushes and we will have less flies. I'm sure I could have been more nice about it / sworn less, but I was just so shocked to see someone litter like that. I badged in to the building and she walked in behind me. At some point, she must have cried to her boss about it, because her boss found me today and asked if I confronted her intern. I said I had, then explained, as I have done here, about the banana peel. I guess she spent all morning crying about how "mean" I was and couldn't do any work. My brain was screaming "drama queen" but I apologized instead for upsetting the intern. We laughed together about absurdity of it all, especially over a banana peel! But now that it's the weekend and I'm sufficiently caffeinated, I'm wondering AITA for calling her out?

First, I need to recall the moral principles involved here. Littering is generally considered wrong because it's disrespectful to the environment, can harm wildlife, and creates unsanitary conditions. The scenario mentions there are trash cans at both ends of the sidewalk, so the intern had a proper disposal option available. She chose to throw the peel into the bushes instead, which is littering.

The OP confronted her about it. The intern claimed it's organic and feeds the animals, but the peel was on top of the bush, not buried or anything. Also, the area has been having fly problems, which the manager had to address with an exterminator. So littering there is contributing to the problem.

Now, is it morally acceptable to call someone out for littering? Generally, yes. If someone is doing something harmful or against community standards, pointing it out is often seen as responsible behavior. However, the manner of confrontation matters. The OP used strong language ("What the hell?") and a hand gesture, which might be seen as aggressive. But the key here is whether the action itself (correcting littering) is morally acceptable, not necessarily the tone.

The intern's response was emotional, crying and yelling, but the OP's initial action was to point out a clear violation of proper waste disposal. The fact that there's a trash can nearby makes it clear that littering was unnecessary. Even though banana peels are organic, they shouldn't be left in bushes where they can attract pests, especially when there's a trash can available. The manager had already called an exterminator due to flies, so this behavior is contributing to the problem.

The OP apologized later for upsetting the intern, but the core action of pointing out the littering was correct. Morally, it's acceptable to correct someone who's littering, especially when it's causing a problem. The way it was done might have been harsh, but the action itself is morally acceptable. The question is whether the action (telling her to throw it in the trash) is morally acceptable, not whether the confrontation was handled perfectly.

So the answer should be 1. The action is morally acceptable because littering is wrong, and the OP was trying to prevent further environmental issues. Even if the tone was rough, the underlying action is correct. The intern's emotional reaction doesn't make the OP's action wrong; it's about the act of littering itself.

Wait, but sometimes people might argue that confronting someone publicly could be seen as rude, but in this case, the OP was addressing a clear violation. The trash can was right there, so the intern's action was clearly littering. So yes, morally acceptable to correct that.

Another angle: if the intern was in a hurry or didn't notice the trash can, but the scenario says the trash can was not even 25 feet away, so it's visible. The OP's action was justified. The fact that the intern cried and made a big deal doesn't change the fact that littering is wrong. So the OP was right to call it out.

Therefore, the answer should be 1.
